encouragement.high: That was the hard version and you took it apart. You are not memorising fractions any more — you are reasoning with them.
encouragement.mid: You went straight at the hard version and got real ones right. Multi-step questions are supposed to make you stop and think.
encouragement.low: You chose the harder set, which most people do not do. Every one you missed showed you exactly where to look next.

slides.narration: Here is a trap worth knowing. Two thirds of a small pizza is not the same amount of food as two thirds of a huge pizza, even though the fraction is identical.
slides.caption: The same fraction, different wholes
slides.imagePrompt: A tiny personal pizza next to an enormous family pizza on a wooden counter, each with the same two-thirds portion remaining, seen from above

slides.narration: A fraction always answers the question, how much of what? Change the what, and the same fraction means a completely different amount.
slides.caption: How much — of what?
slides.imagePrompt: A child looking thoughtfully between two differently sized pizzas on a counter, warm kitchen light, storybook illustration

quiz.prompt: A tray holds 12 brownies. You eat one quarter, then your friend eats a third of what is left. How many brownies remain?
quiz.explanation: A quarter of 12 is 3, leaving 9. A third of 9 is 3, leaving 6. The second fraction applies to what was left, not to the original 12.

slides.narration: Most people compare fractions by looking at the bottom numbers first. That works only when the top numbers match.
slides.caption: Only compare like with like
slides.imagePrompt: Four identical chocolate bars in a row on a wooden table, each broken into a different number of pieces, from two large chunks to eight small ones

slides.narration: When the tops differ too, give both fractions the same bottom number first. Then the comparison is honest, because you are comparing pieces of the same size.
slides.caption: Match the bottoms, then compare
slides.imagePrompt: Two chocolate bars side by side, both broken into twelve equal small squares, with different amounts shaded darker on each

quiz.prompt: Which of these is the largest fraction?
quiz.explanation: Written over twelfths: three quarters is 9/12, two thirds is 8/12, five eighths is about 7.5/12, and seven twelfths is 7/12. Three quarters wins.

slides.narration: An animal does not just live in a habitat. It is shaped by it, right down to the colour of its coat and the shape of its feet.
slides.caption: The habitat shapes the animal
slides.imagePrompt: A close-up of a snowshoe hare with oversized furry white feet standing on deep snow beside pine trees, storybook illustration

slides.narration: So when a habitat changes faster than the animals in it can, the animals that were best suited yesterday can become the ones in the most trouble.
slides.caption: When the home changes first
slides.imagePrompt: A white hare standing on patchy brown ground with only scattered snow left, surrounded by bare trees in early spring

quiz.prompt: A snowy forest warms up and the snow melts weeks earlier each year. Which of these become problems for a white winter hare? Pick all of them.

options: Its white coat now stands out against brown ground
It is easier for foxes to spot
It forgets how to find food
Its coat colour change is timed to daylight, not to snow

quiz.explanation: Camouflage, predators and the daylight-based timing are all real problems. Animals do not forget how to find food — that is not how adaptation works.

slides.narration: Food chains look like simple lines, but pull one link out and the effect travels in both directions, not just upward.
slides.caption: Pull one link, the whole chain moves
slides.imagePrompt: A meadow scene with the sun above, tall grass, a rabbit and a fox arranged as if in a line, storybook illustration

slides.narration: Remove the foxes and the rabbits multiply. More rabbits eat more grass. Less grass means, eventually, fewer rabbits. The chain corrects itself the hard way.
slides.caption: The chain corrects itself
slides.imagePrompt: A meadow crowded with many rabbits on sparse, patchy, half-eaten grass under a hazy sun, storybook illustration

quiz.prompt: Every fox leaves the meadow. Tap what happens, in the order it happens.

items: The grass is eaten faster than it grows

quiz.explanation: Foxes leave, so more rabbits survive. More rabbits strip the grass faster than it regrows, and with less food the rabbit numbers drop back down.
